Welcome coaches, we're very lucky to have Susie Riley join us for our virtual Grand Same Coaches Conference. Susie is from Melbourne, we played much of her tennis in college in America at San Jose State University. Susie has coached players at every stage of the pathway from tennis performance through to professional players. Susie was also the director of tennis at Bolton Arena for 10 years and developed it into one of the leading academies in the UK. The academy was recognised as an LTA International High Performance Centre, awarded to only four academies in the country. Susie is currently coaching WTA player Amari Banks. Now over to Paul Aiken as he takes us on a journey through a Q&A with Susie. Over to you Paul. Absolute pleasure today to have you on Susie. You're a local Melbourne girl, Australian-born, you're a accomplished coach and player, you come from a family of coaches. Just tell us a little bit about your journey. Well, yes, I am from Melbourne and I do come from a family of tennis players, my whole family plays, got coaches in the family as well, so we've definitely played a lot together

as a family and my dad actually was my first coach. Wonderful, wonderful. And who really lit the spark? Was it dad? Was it your brother? Tell us a little bit about that pathway. It was definitely my dad. I was always really fascinated with his own journey of playing and even in the 70s coming over and playing through Europe and so he definitely lit the spark around the playing to a high level and the international travel and he played to a great level but he was also a great coach at bringing that down to my level and really trying to instill what he knew I needed to be doing in me at a young age. Fantastic. And then you went over and you played some college tennis. Tell us a little bit about that. Where did you play and how did you experience that? Oh, I absolutely loved playing college tennis. It was, I knew I wanted to do it from a very young age. I saw a lot of other players at the club or clubs around me that were going. I was at San Jose State and I absolutely loved the experience. I knew I always wanted to go to university and this was a great way to combine playing tennis to a high level, playing division one tennis and combining that with doing my business degree. But it was fantastic because it was a real combination of playing with a team which you don't always get in tennis and then that travelling away was an experience in experiencing different, a lot of different states around America too.

Indeed. And so the college years ended. Tell us a little bit about how you fell, if you like, into performance coaching. Yes, I mean, I actually wasn't going to be a coach. It wasn't something that I was thinking about. I was studying business and I thought I would go down that track. But when I was just thinking about what I was going to do next and was coming home, I played a $25,000 tournament in California and there was another player that was there at the time and we were just hitting partners through that tournament. We were both there for the week. And so we just became friends. I came home after continuing playing college tennis and she went on to have a career playing professionally and 12 months later, I get a call from her and she's coming out to play the Australian Open. And so obviously, very, very well and said, did I want to come and be a hitting partner for her at the Australian Open when I thought I'd love to. So that's kind of how it started, really. Fantastic. And what was her name and how did how did you enjoy the experience of travelling and what sort of mentors did you find across the journey? So her name was Mary of Palatia, so she was Canadian player. And when I came back to Australia, I was starting to do a little bit of coaching and just just on the weekends, I started doing my coaching qualifications. And then this experience with Mary of where I am for the first year

I was just getting with her at the Australian Open. And then it was really the second year when she came out and I'd started to establish my my coaching business and I decided that that's what I wanted to do. That was when she said, did I want to come travelling with her? And so I guess my coaching career is a little bit back to front. I had a fantastic opportunity to travel with a player that was top 200 and really see the game at the highest level and see how coaches were working with players at the highest level. Now, sadly for us in Australia, you've ended up in the UK and it's good luck for them. But you've made your way to Bolton Academy. Can you tell us a little bit about what Bolton Academy is and a little bit about the, I guess, the background of that? Yeah, so basically launching my coaching career with Mary of I was on tour for about three years with with players. And I just thought that with coming across to Europe so much from Australia, I really thought it'd be great if I could base myself in the UK and my brother was coaching in the UK at the time. And so with his contacts, I thought this is a great opportunity to come and base myself in the UK. And then I still wanted to be travelling with pro players. So I came to Manchester and said, where's your biggest academy? And that's when I was directed to Bolton Arena, which actually hosts Team Tannis, which is the lead up to Tarps for the 14 under Tannis Europe events.

Was it in the UK at that time that received funding for performance players? Is that right? Yes. So at that time, there were about 24 centres in the country that the LTA funded. So they were part of that part of that network. And they were at the time they were what was considered a silver status. So there was international high performance, which was the top four centres in the country. And then the 20 that sat below that were gold, silver and bronze. So it was a silver slash bronze performing academy. So it was one of the 24, but it wasn't really performing as one of the best centres in the country. So the opportunity came for you to then take over the play development side of the centre. What did you notice that you could change and how did you identify this? Yes, I mean, it was a great opportunity. I was there for a few months and the opportunity to become director of performance. Tennis came up and so I went for the role and got it. And I guess I could. Yeah, I thought I could really hit the ground running here because I was watching the background for four months while I was working with a professional player out of Bolton, Naomi Brody, who was 17 at the time. And one of the biggest things that I noticed and as you as you asked what I the first thing

I did when I came into the position was actually around the squad structure with all the players in the programme. What I noticed is where there were these small squads made up of three or four players with a coach dotted all around the week. And what I was noticing is, you know, with player progression, with players improving and probably should be moving into other squads, it was just very political with moving them from squads and moving someone out of a squad. And I just saw these decisions being put off with really making sure players were in the right the right squad with the right training environment. So the first thing I put into place when I came in as director of the programme is I got rid of the squad structure and instead put in what I call training days. So, for example, on a on a Tuesday and a Thursday, our under 12 player base, they would come in and we had our we had four courts, 16 players and week on week, if players were progressing, they would be moving up or down courts, depending on the level that they were bringing on the day, but also the level that they were improving throughout throughout the week. So it was the first thing I did and actually probably made the biggest difference, probably in a six month time frame. That's really interesting because it sounds like you took away like almost an elitist or head to head sort of this is an elite squad that almost brought everyone together. Would that be right?

Oh, absolutely. And it was a great it was a great tool for having we did have our top court right down to our court one, right down to court four. But anyone knew that on any day if they were putting in the work ethic that we that we required and we're competitive, we could move them up the court and switch them over and and. Yeah, wow. Yeah. And that the acceleration from that was actually really quite quite surprising. But as you say, it took away all the issues of having to take someone out of a squad and move someone up. We just did it very organically through the session. And always start with a with a mixer of winners, up losers, down in the warm up. So from the very first moment plays was definitely on court in that warm up. They were ready to put their best effort on court. Fabulous. And your pathway, Susie, was quite holistic from what I've led to believe from grassroots all the way up to performance. Tell us a little bit about why that you felt that was so important to actually have that in synergy. Yes, it was really important for me to to really try and home grow our own players and and be able to really accelerate their development and keep building on on their progress. So we we did have our own development program, which led into our under 10 performance program and then 14 and under through to 16 plus, which was your juniors that were playing ITF and our professional full time Academy as well.

Fantastic. And I'm really interested now to digress a little bit into how you created your team, because obviously that's just a pivotal part of any sort of academy, the people that you have in place, making sure that they're in the right place and that they're happy. Can you tell us a little bit about that? Yes, I mean, the team, the reason we were able to achieve everything we did was because we had an excellent team all working really closely together. And we the whole team had bought into what we were trying to achieve. So I mean, from day one, I set out a strategic plan that really set the scene with what we were all trying to achieve. But in each of those areas, I I went out and recruited coaches that had a track record of really developing in those areas. So it was very key to bring in a very good coach to lead our ten under program, who has done that journey, many times bringing through players through to a national level, ready to ready for that international journey. So recruiting players or recruiting coaches at each stage of that pathway was was very was key to our success, really. And they were just coaches that you'd met across the journey or did you actively sort them out? Yeah, how did you do that?

Yes, so I I knew who I wanted as part of the team. So I it's in I didn't go out and rush out to early spring in this team. It was probably within that first year that I I brought in my my first key coach in that ten under stage to really get that going. And then I took that first year to really seek out who I wanted. But it was definitely a head hunting recruitment process, but also developing within. So after about three years, I actually developed a junior coach in our program. I was mentoring him over a three four year period, and he actually became head of our men's program. So there was a combination of me mentoring coaches into key positions and recruiting coaches with a track record. And you mentioned in a prior conversation that we had about how important it was to really value and validate some great things that your your coaches do with players. How did you do that? So I think the kind of key to success with this passing on of players comes from recognition. So with our under 10 program, we had we had a coaching team doing a brilliant job. And I needed them year on year to keep doing that brilliant job of passing through to the next group of coaches that knew the journey at that 12 and under and 40 and under tennis year at level. So recognition was one of our key values that I tried to bring to life in every meeting that we had weekly. So a great example of this is we had a player who did very well at Targ's one year.

So a 14 year old player. And when we talked about successes of our players, that coach really talked about the serve of this particular player and how they dominated with their serve. And and I highlighted that that player back in our 10 and under program worked so hard on getting those fundamentals right, because we knew that this play would have the serve would be a fundamental part of their game for the future. So our 10 and under team worked very hard on developing the fundamentals of this serve. So in the coaches meeting, I went back to that story and said, how fantastic that we've seen this play out now at Targ's. And that was developed by the great work that you did in the 10 and under program. And that was something that I tried to do and have the team do quite a lot of really recognizing the work as a team we were all doing. That's absolutely fantastic. My my thoughts as well is that people like to keep developing as well and learning themselves. So what sort of opportunities did you provide for those coaches? So coach development is is really, really important. And even for myself and I'm I'm really hungry to keep learning and insane and seeing where the future of the game is going and what does that mean for our development of our younger players? So what I what I did with the with the coaching team is we had a weekly meeting for every Monday morning and the entire coaching team needed to come to that.

And that was a chance for us all to get on court and highlight the key things we were doing in our age groups and we would get on court. We'd go through drills and it was a chance to really have all the senior coaches upskill our junior coaches. So just really talking about key teaching points and how to regress or progress different drills. And so I found that by us all coming together and all of us like using our experience to help the junior coaches coming through was one way. But the second the second thing that I did in those coaches meetings is monthly I would have a coach present. So any of our coaches that went off and did courses or workshops or were at an international event or a national event, I wanted them to come back and and and tell us about it and upscale the rest of the coaching team. So it was very much we're all trying to do what we know we need to do, but we need to be learning from each other and bringing back really good practice. Absolutely. Yeah, that's so cool. I want to touch on now a little bit about the mechanics of the program and what sort of now like competitive opportunities did you have for the players? And I guess how did you individualize their programs? Yes, I mean, it's it's not easy being over here in the UK. We've got Europe on out on our doorstep. So I mean, that's a fantastic opportunity. And it's something that's a lot more difficult for the players in Australia.

So we knew what needed to be in place and where rankings needed to be to hit those ranking targets and hit their individual development plan goals. Yeah, that's so cool. Just for yourself. So I would seek out mentors and so probably no formal mentors, but I was always seeking out those that had done it before me. So I was on the phone to him saying, what lessons did you learn if you could do it all over again? How would you do things differently? And tried to really take as much from his experience of heading up the academy and being very successful.

So from that point of view, I'd seek out performance directors of other academies. But then because I've been working with WTA players, I would also seek out successful WTA coaches and just really ask them and inquire as to what worked, what didn't work, what strategies did they use. And so I did a lot of seeking out, trying to just be very inquisitive and try and learn as much as I can from those that had done it and that I could really follow or learn from them. That's amazing. Just getting back a little bit to the mechanics of the program again. I'm going to be remiss for me not to ask how you manage parental expectation and how do you educate the parents along this journey. So something I set out again in my first year and it was something that when I asked all the other performance directors, it's like, what is the biggest problem that you have? And they said, parents. And I mean, parents can offer so much to a program if they're managed in the right way. And so I tried to tackle that right at the beginning. So I set out for the Academy a communication framework. So it was really clear to parents how they could communicate with the team and how we would communicate with them. So it was very clear almost that to give an example of if there was any issues, parents first would go to their individual coach and then their coordinator. If they were saying they attended under program

and then they would come through to me. So there was a very clear order of how. So that communication framework, it was a very useful tool because if I then suddenly got an email out of the blue, I could go back with and say, if you speak first to your individual coach and then your coordinator, you may be able to get the answers that you need. And it was just a way of, and that happened early, but then the parents all got to understand that framework in which we all needed to work and respect each other. But the parent education part was also really important. So I would run, every month we had parent education workshops on loads of different areas from how does the performance pathway, what does it look like, the competition structure, even down to probably one of the most successful ones I ran was in Bolton Arena, we have a balcony or the parents are watching. And one of the workshops I ran was for this next month, this is our curriculum, this is what we're delivering on court, this is what you'll see. And it just almost, because it could see them looking down and wanting to be involved. And I thought, if they just understand and know what we're doing, they can just sit back and relax a little bit. So that was a great one. So we off the back of that did quite a few around our curriculum. So parents knew what was coming and knew what they could expect to see on court. Yeah, that sounds incredible.

Because I think, as a parent, you just want sort of transparency of what's going to happen, what's coming up. And it sounds like you had an amazing structure for that. Speaking of which, we've got a few coaches obviously will be listening into this or watching us. And if you had three things that they could do to replicate what you've done with your academy, what would they be? So if they're an academy coach working with a very similar role to Bolton, the number one thing I would say is strategic planning. You need to absolutely know what you're trying to achieve and by when. And if you know what you're trying to achieve, then it's just about mapping out that journey so that you can track, evaluate, adapt, make iterations. If you don't know exactly what you're trying to achieve, then it's really hard to achieve. So that's the number one thing is that strategic planning of what it is that you're trying to achieve and how you're going to do it. But the second thing which actually follows on from that is I have seen a lot of coaches actually do a really good job around that planning where I think they can fall down is actually evaluating. So really understanding how if you've set a goal, have you really achieved that goal? And if you haven't, you need to understand why and you need to make changes except evaluation side of things. And that crosses over into players. So and I think my third part of that is around player progress

Well, what I love about the journey of working with Marnie is that Marnie started in our program when she was four years old. And so she has actually come through my whole pathway. At 15, she actually went to Spain and did, there was a whole structure change in the LTA with funding. So it was a good opportunity for her to go abroad. So she spent a couple of years in Spain training full-time at the Spanish Academy. But I love the fact that she came right through our junior program, right through to 15. And then she's now come back and I've started working with her.

But again, going back to your question with Marnie, is I mapped out that journey. That's of no surprise that she's achieved that 500 ranking because it was mapped out. And we watched what she needed to be doing, her development goals, her competition structure that would allow her the points to achieve that ranking. So again, for next year, we've actually mapped out that for next year, it's pushing her to 250. And then the next part of our plan is for her to move into top 50. So that first year, even though it hasn't completely gone to plan, because she actually had three months out with a back injury in the early part of the year. So again, with all players and with planning, things don't always go to plan, but it's that adapting to what happens. Yeah, what I think is amazing is that throughout this conversation, you've got a very structured approach, which is a proven winner for you, because even from what you said previously about the strategic planning,

that's just related. That's an example of that with Imani's great form at the moment. It's all been planned. You've got a very staged approach, which is just fabulous. Out of all the players that you've worked with, who's someone that's really surprised you, that's come out of the box? It's just had great individual improvement. It's actually a player in that it's actually a national example, so it's not an international example. But again, it goes back to this planning, actually, because there was a group of players, and I was working with a professional player at the time, and she was off travelling. So I saw a bunch of girls, and a player stood out to me, and she was 16. She was very tall, but was playing two metres behind the baseline, so just didn't have a game style that suited her, and she had weapons, but she wasn't in a position to use any weapons. So I had an opportunity to work with her for three months within the programme, and again said, I think we could really turn things around for you if you buy into changing the way you play. And so she went in a three-month period. We mapped out what we were going to do, and of course, I got her buy-in, because nothing works unless you get the buy-in from the player. Absolutely. And in three months, she went from equivalent of, we call them grade threes over here, but a regional level tournament. So she was playing regionally

and just getting into some national tournaments. Three months later, she had got into qualities of nationals and was in the final of nationals and lost in the final of nationals in a three-month period of being at regional tournaments to almost winning nationals. I mean, that would have been a very tale story for her. But she really surprised me because of... Well, I was just very impressed with how she could decide at that stage in the game to play completely differently and to really trust the process and work at it for three months and then for her to get that reward and see that level of achievement for her. I thought that was a great example of, yes, again, the strategic planning, but really getting that buy-in from the player and then seeing that success. Yes, and I think so many coaches have just resonated with that because it's really for a lot of people. And I can't speak for everyone, but it's not about the money. It's about these sort of stories where you just see, regardless of the level, you just see this amazing improvement and you're just so happy for the person. It's a real team effort. So look, that's just incredible. Tell us a little bit about now. What's potentially coming up next, what you'd like to do, and I guess exactly what you're doing now. So there's a few things. I'm working, obviously, with Amani Banks and where she's just going into her pre-season now.

So we're ready to hopefully, in January, hit the ground running for her to achieve her top 250 goal, which you can watch that space.
